items.body: Simi Fyda‘s In My Personal Heaven, I’m the Devil’s Spawn offers no gentle introduction. Compared to Yuri (2023), it works within a noticeably narrower palette. The bright contrasts of its predecessor have given way to a largely monochrome world, built from minute variations of timbre, pressure and pitch. Many of the preoccupations of Yuri remain, but they are pursued with greater concentration. The music repeatedly folds back on itself, testing how much tension can be extracted from the smallest amount of material. The opening track, “-may-care”, signals a state of abrasion, establishing an atmosphere of metallic coldness that hangs over the entire record. “maso chords” introduces a faint current of nostalgia, its harmonies carrying the suggestion of something remembered yet irretrievable. From there, the material grows steadily more compressed. “idle hands” simmers without release, while “hedo chords” circles obsessively around recurring intervals and frozen harmonic figures. By the time “mono chords” arrives, repetition itself has become the subject. Minute tonal inflections slowly reshape the surface until the music seems to trap itself inside its own logic, producing a sense of claustrophobia without ever resorting to excess. Originally conceived as an octophonic installation before being reimagined for stereo, the music acquires an unusually enclosed character. Sounds seem unable to disperse, and repeated gestures linger, each return carrying greater psychological weight. Even the faint vocal traces remain caught within the surrounding texture, surfacing only briefly before dissolving back into the dense harmonic field. The closing “take the hindmost” provides the only substantial shift in perspective. Layers of electronic residue and circuitry redirect attention towards texture itself, as if searching for a new vocabulary from within the material already at hand. Nothing resolves. Instead, the album erases its own traces, leaving behind only the memory of sounds unwilling to disappear. The allow us to delve deeper into her personal heaven, Simi Fyda has kindly agreed to answer four questions by email. The album emerged from what you describe as “a version that almost existed” — music composed during a period of isolation and then reshaped into its final form. Could you talk about what was lost, what was retained, and whether you think traces of that unrealised version still haunt the record we hear today? I started the octophonic pieces during a period where I genuinely couldn’t make anything. I had no access to whatever I normally rely on. So I thought okay, let’s see if I still can do this. It was less of a decision and more just something to do, or to maintain. When I came back to it I was still kinda fed up with the whole thing, which actually helped. I stopped being careful with it and a lot got cut. But the atmosphere stayed, which annoyed me at first because I half wanted a clean break from it. I think that the earlier version is still in there somewhere, not as a foundation, probably more like the thing the record keeps almost touching without quite getting there. You have said that composing this music felt like becoming a demon — specifically one of the figures your grandmother claimed to have encountered in the very space where the album was eventually completed. How did that family story enter the work, and what does the title In My Personal Heaven, I’m the Devil’s Spawn reveal about the relationship between ancestry, memory, and self-transformation in your practice? I moved back into my grandmother’s apartment last November for a couple months and basically just disappeared into it. I wasn’t planning to make a record about any of that. I thought I was making something from a place rather than about it. She had paranoid schizophrenia, periods of seeing figures, demons, specific presences in specific corners of that apartment. I grew up hearing all of it, kind of terrified and fascinated at the same time. I lived there alone as a teenager too. So by the time I came back last november, it was already carrying a lot, I just wasn’t thinking about it consciously. She died in March, right after the album was finished. The timing still felt… I don’t even have a word to use here to be honest. The album isn’t about her, at least that wasn’t the intention. But she’s in there. Much of the album feels remarkably restrained. Tracks seem to hover on the verge of unleashing a full sonic assault, yet repeatedly pull back into themselves. Even the buried vocal traces feel half-suppressed, as though emerging from behind a wall. Was this tension between eruption and containment a conscious compositional strategy, or did it arise naturally from the material? Mostly conscious. I over-anticipate everything. I’ll have already resolved something in my head before it’s even happened, which just kills it. So a lot of this was genuinely trying not to do that. Whenever something felt like it was building toward release I’d just hold it there a bit longer than felt comfortable. I kept reminding myself that circling around something can be enough, that I don’t always have to arrive, don’t have to control every outcome in the ways I’ve conditioned myself to. The record is built around recurrence rather than development, with sounds, intervals, pipe tones and microtonal clusters reappearing in altered forms throughout the album. Given your background in installation and spatial sound, how did the process of collapsing an octophonic work into stereo affect your thinking about repetition, space and listening? Did reducing the physical dimensions of the piece paradoxically make it feel more intimate, claustrophobic, or psychologically charged? The recurrence came from spending a long time with a very small pool of material. At some point development just stopped making sense as a framework. Returning somehow did. In the octophonic versions sound could leave, it had a room to dissolve into. In stereo it couldn’t, so everything that was previously escapable became structural. The noise, the density, all of it just stayed there and then I brought it all even closer and it changed what the material actually was. I think space didn’t disappear, it just stopped being outside the work.

items.body: Somatic Responses and John Healy, specifically on this release, have spent over three decades refining the specific space between force and sweetness that their catalog occupies. Operational Ambivalence doesn’t reinvent that space. It just inhabits it with the kind of confidence that comes from thirty years of knowing exactly where you live. Force and sweetness intertwined Operational Ambivalence by Somatic Responses   Brothers John and Paul Healy have been operating as Somatic Responses out of Ammanford, a small industrial mining community in southwest Wales, since 1994. They formed in the hardcore acid techno scene, releasing their first material in 1995 before gradually expanding into industrial, drum and bass, noise, ambient, and breakcore territory. Their 1999 debut Circumflex on Hymen Records was a pivotal moment—taking their sound into new levels of complexity and intensity, and subsequent releases on Ad Noiseam, Sublight, Component, and their own Photon Emissions label built one of the most expansive and underappreciated catalogs in hard-edged electronic music. Key influence on rhythmic noise, breakcore, and IDM, yet somehow always operating just below the mainstream radar. The duo describe their work as “complex dislocated and broken beats, distorted intelligent constructions, fascinating sonic structures, force and sweetness intertwined.” Operational Ambivalence, it’s worth noting, credits “Everything by J.S.Healy“—making this a solo John Healy production, recorded in the Macro Chamber in Ammanford, rather than a full duo effort. The distinction is subtle but real. What you get with Operational Ambivalence is largely what you’d expect from the Somatic Responses catalog: distortion, drums, hectic patterns with beautiful ambience woven throughout. It’s a 14-track self-released collection that feels like a gathering of material that belongs together rather than a concept album with a rigid arc. Tracks 8, 9, and 14 are the more ambient pieces of the release and still create beautiful visual imagery through technique. Out of that ambient batch, “H doesn’t fall down the stairs…” is the most interesting—not strictly ambient like the other two, but considerably softer in production than everything surrounding it. The lightness and strange composition here is compelling in its subtlety, drum rhythm play with light percussion and glitched patterns that sit between experimental and delicate. Distortion, drums, hectic patterns with beautiful ambience woven throughout :: “New Shift” is another standout, with its intro of rolling clicks and sounds moving left to right across the stereo field, slowly manipulated kick drums coming in gradually as the track builds rhythm. What you thought was a softer track reveals itself as something larger entirely. The technique of building anticipation through percussion here is notable, it recalls the way Lexaunculpt constructed his pattern builds of glitches and various percussions on The Blurring of Trees (Planet Mu, 2003), that same slow accumulation of rhythmic detail until the structure reveals itself. The patterns here are interesting and the execution is patient. “Gatch” is another standout in all of its distortion and drumming. What makes it work compositionally is how it messes with pattern recognition, introducing drum patterns that redirect where you expect the track to go. The distortion is toned down carefully, which is harder than it sounds. Somatic Responses have always been comfortable in distortion’s territory, and John Healy demonstrates that comfort here, using strong distortion without making ears bleed, keeping it controlled enough that it serves the composition rather than overwhelming it. Using strong distortion without making ears bleed :: “Vital Ex Parts 1 and 2” earns its nine-minute runtime—two parts that feel like one extended piece assembled well. The drums in the introduction are playful before they introduce harsher builds, eventually transforming into something darker with ambient surroundings closing in. And “Residual Behaviour” is the track that’s hardest not to stop at simply because of how oddly it stands out in the context of everything else. Real drum samples playing in broken patterns with chords filling in the background—it sounds off, but there’s a strange beauty to it. The double hits, the stutters, the subtle chords and notes behind the rhythm, there’s no steady pulse here, just experimentation. When a rhythm starts forming it plays briefly before switching again, until the track ends on skips and rolls and hi-hats leading the outro with swishy drums. It sounds like it was a genuinely fun track to make, and that energy comes through in the listening. Somatic Responses and John Healy, specifically on this release, have spent over three decades refining the specific space between force and sweetness that their catalog occupies. Operational Ambivalence doesn’t reinvent that space. It just inhabits it with the kind of confidence that comes from thirty years of knowing exactly where you live. Artwork once again by Mattia Travaglini, whose visual language has become as much a part of the Somatic Responses aesthetic as the music itself. Operational Ambivalence is available on Bandcamp. Operational Ambivalence by Somatic ResponsesThe post Somatic Responses :: Operational Ambivalence (Self Released) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: Kine 3 is a newer sound built off the classic. Roel Funcken has described the Kine series as emerging from a need to process a large body of work—dividing material into categories, finding what felt raw and process-driven and unfinished in the best possible way. A producer still genuinely curious about what his machines will do next Kine 3 by Roel Funcken   The golden era of IDM left behind a particular kind of silence, not the absence of music, but the absence of the restless, process-driven curiosity that made that era feel alive. What’s left of it now echoes through the electronic music landscape in small signals, from old and new artists working in the margins. Roel Funcken has been one of those signals for over two decades, and Kine 3 is his loudest transmission yet—a massive tracklist, a substantial runtime, and the third installment of an ongoing series that began as a way of making sense of a large body of work. The Kine series, released through EC Underground—the South Florida-based multidisciplinary collective and label that has been bridging European and UK electronic music to US audiences since 2018, operates on a process-first logic: raw, modular, driven by hardware and intention rather than polish and structure. My first encounter with Roel‘s work came through a college radio station playing Funckarma‘s Part 3 EP on Djak-Up-Bitch, the Rotterdam-based Dutch label specializing in modern electronica and IDM distributed through Clone. That particular series was something, the melodic play and drum work had a freshness that aged remarkably well, still sounds lovely today. Fast forward years later and here we land with Kine 3. This album shows the maturity of Roel as a solo artist, distinct from the Funckarma project that first put him on the map alongside his brother Don. His productions here aren’t built around melodic composition in the conventional IDM sense, they’re explorative and experimental, each track following a particular pattern of letting effects and drums do the talking while atmospheric or melodic backgrounds grind immersively in the background. The loop continues :: With a tracklist this expansive, the best approach is to section it. Tracks 1 through 8 share similarities in style and composition — drums and effects leading, melodies surfacing immersively rather than announcing themselves. What Funcken does here shouldn’t be misread as pure improvisation. It’s closer to freeplay with intention, a distinction that matters. Modular synthesis and process-driven production naturally produce moments that feel unplanned, but behind every patch decision is a set of deliberate choices: which modules are connected, what triggers what, where the randomness is allowed and where it’s controlled. Funcken‘s approach on Kine 3 sits in that exact space—the results sound alive and unpredictable but the architecture holding them together is clearly considered. Track 9, “4ehmth,” functions as a divider. It’s the only track of the bunch that’s almost entirely drum play, and whether intentional or not, it creates a natural break between the first and second halves of the album. “Bydow 32” carries a distinct Funckarma feeling—a reminiscence of “Atomic” or “Finsbury Park” from Part 3, those same loose, melodic textures surfacing again through a different production context. “Dorphins” is another standout. Its melodic structure separates itself from the rest of the batch because the tweaking of the melody is being granularized at fast speeds, bouncing on a single note with harsh portamento bend stabs cutting through. Portamento—the gliding between pitches rather than jumping discretely, becomes a compositional tool here rather than just an effect. When applied fast and aggressively, it creates a pitch tension that sits between melody and noise, which is exactly what Funcken is exploiting. The drum structure across all these tracks is consistently loose and abrasive, not a loop so much as one long continuous rhythm that plays through rather than repeating. The two bonus digital tracks round things out distinctly. “Koidz” is heavier—distorted drums, more rhythmically aggressive than the core album, with a crunchy acid bass and what sounds like significant knob movement throughout. The emotional pads that come in give it a melodic tone that sticks to the structure as it plays, a ringing atmospheric pad leading the melody in a way the main album rarely does. “Kido” takes the same sound palette and reconfigures it—a different melodic composition built from similar material but toned differently, another take on the same logic but with its own feel of rhythm and structure. Kine 3 is a newer sound built off the classic. Roel Funcken has described the Kine series as emerging from a need to process a large body of work—dividing material into categories, finding what felt raw and process-driven and unfinished in the best possible way. He noted that sitting back and listening to Kine 1 with an audience changed something: the distance it created meant he was actually listening rather than judging. The support those releases received went straight back into the system—new Eurorack modules, extending the loop. Kine 3 is what that loop sounds like three iterations in, and it sounds exactly like what it is: a producer still genuinely curious about what his machines will do next, documenting the results with the confidence of someone who’s been doing this long enough to know when to get out of the way and let the process speak. EC Underground found the right home for it. The loop continues. Kine 3 is available on EC Underground. items.body: Review by blessed_of — Compassionizer tribute to Depeche Mode is a sincere and beautifully crafted homage that captures the emotional depth and melodic power of the original songs, while reimagining them through the band's unique avant-prog and ambient sensibility. Instead of simply reproducing familiar material, Compassionizer opens new dimensions?experimenting with texture, rhythm, and atmosphere to make each piece feel newly discovered. "But Not Tonight" opens the album with a warm, dreamy atmosphere. Where Depeche Mode's version glows with youthful melancholy, Compassionizer transforms it into a reflective meditation. "World Full of Nothing" and "The Things You Said" follow with chamber-like arrangements and subtle electronics, preserving the emotional fragility of the originals while reframing them through the band's layered and expressive sound. "Blue Dress" maintains the sensual minimalism of Depeche Mode but becomes more introspective and ethereal, while "Sibeling" expands into a sweeping ambient dialogue between piano, clarinet, and electronic textures. The closing "Enjoy the Silence" stands not as a cover but as a reimagining?slower, sacred, and contemplative. Where Depeche Mode's originals thrive on sleek synth- pop precision, Compassionizer adds warmth, introspection, and organic depth, creating not imitation but an honest conversation across time and genres. A beautiful, thoughtful, and deeply moving album.

Two tracks, in particular, have made a lasting impression: "I Feel Shine of the Day" and "For the Invisible Things." The album, as a whole, feels like an intricate journey, crafted with immense care and dedication. It's clear that Compassionizer has invested a great deal of effort, resources, and time into creating this project. From the very first note to the final soundscape, you can sense the precision and intentionality behind each element. The group's ability to weave together diverse sounds and moods is truly remarkable, giving each track its own unique character while maintaining a cohesive narrative throughout. One of the most striking aspects of "The Fellowship of the Mystery" is the band's ongoing evolution. With every album, Compassionizer continues to refine and expand their sound, pushing boundaries and experimenting with new ideas. Their growth as artists is evident in this latest release, which feels like a natural progression from their previous work while also introducing fresh and innovative elements. What I particularly love about this album is its ability to transport the listener into different emotional states. "I Feel Shine of the Day" is a radiant, uplifting track that seems to encapsulate the essence of hope and light, while "For the Invisible Things" taps into more subtle, introspective emotions. The band's commitment to their craft is palpable, and it's exciting to see where they will go from here as they continue to evolve and refine their sound. This is a must-listen for anyone who appreciates deep, thoughtful, and emotionally charged music.

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — Mental Architects are a very interesting math rock band from Bulgaria, that is unfortunately nolonger active. The trio consisting of Tony Velev (guitars), Nikki Ranguelov (bass), and MaxStoimenov (drums) tackles a rhythmically complex style that is simultaneously melodic, light-hearted, and digestible. Unlike many contemporary names in the math rock scene, MA have the peculiartendency to write fun and catchy sophisticated music, as you will often hear neat riffs and grooved-out chords on their 2012 studio album 'Celebrations', which is officially their third outing. Thereis an ostensible yet subtle post-rock aftertaste all over this record, but definitely not in theform of otherworldly crescendos or extended solos. The album is pretty playful and energetic, and tomy ears, one of the few math rock collections that could make you want to... dance?Why not; after all this is a celebratory album that impresses with a vast and flourishing guitarsound, often enough relying on multiple lines working around each other (this is a strong studioproject, above all), while the bass guitar and the drums, as tasty as they are, remain lessprominent, or even a little restrained, if you will. Had the band been more fusion-oriented, therhythm section could have been more unconventional and more prone to experimentation, but MentalArchitects' music is incredibly enjoyable, nonetheless. The compositions that certainly impress meon this album are 'Spell Shelter', 'Here Is Where, Where Better' (respectively the first and secondtracks), the 7-minute-long 'Ace of Keys', which is mesmerizing, and the song called 'Meth-Rock',which appears towards the end of the album. There is a joyous warmth to the music on 'Celebrations',which will appeal to many listeners, but that album cover... it's just alright.

items.body: Review by Agnenrecords — Delirium's sixth studio album Sesta strada lungo il tempo (Sixth Road Through Time) was released in May this year, with a line-up similar to that responsible for 2015's L'Era della Menzogna, Enrico Tixi replacing drummer Alfredo Vandresi. It's not a concept album but references to the band's previous output, snapshots of time, characters and places, all create a series of linked stories embellished with a sense of Liguria and the sea.Opening with a multipart side-long track Schiavo della vilt� (Slave of Cowardice), it's obvious that the group are in full-on prog mode. The piece concerns itself with the morals of warfare through a protagonist who witnesses, and takes part in the horrors of war, knowing the acts are evil but is unable to speak out against them out of fear for what would happen to him. He reflects on leaving his lover behind as he sets off for war, and on the futility of conflict, the lives lost, never to dream, love or be free again. He finds his deeds shameful while his fellow soldiers seem to revel in the bloodshed in the name of the national flag. Musically, it fits together really well; different moods correspond to different sections and the lyrics, which recall Tremori antichi (from Lo scemo e il villaggio), are delivered with Corvaglia's dramatic vocals. Io clochard (I'm a Homeless Person) begins 'beyond the snow', blood-stained snow having featured in Schiavo della vilt�. A few bars of plaintive strings reflect the hardships of the protagonist; the dusty road and stale, mouldy bread that still tastes good, an indication that the perceived tribulations aren't unbearable. He's got his dog as a companion, time to rest and reflect, and a destination: the sea. The music primarily consists of a dense repeated phrase with a bubbly bass adding some colour, overlain with short saxophone breaks and a brief guitar solo, and guest vocalist Alice Vigo repeats the final verse in French.Il riposo del pirata (The Pirate's Rest) begins with ambient seashore sounds. Electric piano is employed in a rhythmic context, and saxophone and synthesizer weave around the vocal melody describing an old pirate in an old hammock, cradling a tankard of rum and listening to a song he can hear on the wind. Martial music indicates the final rest of the pirate and there'll be no more looting of treasure. The voices of the pirate crew can be discerned underneath Corvaglia's announcement, speaking in English: "I don't know what to do" and "I've had enough of this". Short organ sax and solos precede the final spoken verse, describing the crew celebrating the valour of the pirate on the sand where the waves bring in light foam reminiscent of freshly poured beer.Della strada il ritorno (On the Road Back) is a jazzy instrumental, beginning with string bass and piano. The piece has a real swing and there's a pleasing rhythmic complexity with Grice's saxophone soloing over the drums, bass and piano. A series of solos, energetic guitar, slower paced bass, flute, piano and sax complete the tune.Parole nel vento (Words in the Wind) has a fairly straightforward opening, before a flute riff, backed by hard rhythmic intervals, leads the song into Jethro Tull-like territory. I'm reminded of Corvaglia's track Il cerchio del comando on S.E.I. by La Maschera di Cera, which I've previously described as being like a Delirium song. Vigo shines on a lead synthesizer line that could have been performed by Keith Emerson, and following the last two vocal lines the band indulge in a blues blow out until the end of the song. While the lyrical content seems to reference both Il nome del vento ("The words thrown into the wind, who will listen?") and L'Era della Menzogna ("An ageless story made of a few lies and illusions mixed with fake freedom"), the track feels like it's pulling the strands of the four preceding stories together, creating a perfect ending.The whole album makes an enjoyable listen. It's well-crafted with a very high standard musicianship and production, expertly blending a distinct feel of past Delirium albums with an updated sound. Highly recommended.(This review originally appeared as part of a Delirium band history/album review on progblog.co.uk)

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — A retrospective that deserves the attention and respect that its subject, David "Axe" Axelrod does. The only problem I have with this album is the glaring omission of his work with Julian "Cannonball" Adderley ("Mercy, Mercy, Mercy"!), the absence of anything from the two albums Capitol Records commissioned David to produce (and compose music for) by the "failing" Electric Prunes--two albums that are now recognized as leading lights of the 1960s Psychedelic era of music (and culture). Otherwise I am very happy with the attempt to raise consciousness of Axe's significant contributions to pop, jazz, and funk musics. A book should be written about this passionate, haunted, and fearless man--a true champion and loud advocate of human rights, civil rights, and care and attention to the wronged, down-trodden, dispossessed, oppressed, and marginalized.I also love the fact that there are songs of David's presented here that I'd never heard before. It could have been a double or triple album!

items.body: Review by ken_scrbrgh — There is an irony that I am considering Steve Howe's, "Beginnings," after ruminating over the four other Yes' solo albums released in 1975-1976: Howe's was the first to make its premiere. "Authentic" is the adjective I would like to employ in pondering this album almost fifty-one years after its emergence."Yesfreak" that I was back then and now, I must admit that, unlike Chris Squire's, "Fish Out of Water," I was not drawn to "Beginnings." In truth, for many years, I was seriously familiar only with Squire's album. Only since 2023, have I thoroughly come to appreciate Anderson, White, and Moraz' efforts. I would venture Howe's record emerged first in 1975 as the result of the solo work he maintained parallel to his work with Yes. I have to speculate that during the conception and initial execution of the pieces destined to yield "Beginnings," Howe chose to sing the lead vocals. Perhaps, then, as a matter of economy and facilitation, he opted to retain his lead vocal performances? If we consider 2023's, "Mirror to the Sky" and this year's, "Aurora," we encounter "successful" lead vocals from Howe on, "Unknown Place" and "Countermovement." Surely, though, in the mid-Seventies, Howe's lead vocals on his first solo album attenuated attention given to this effort.Then and now this lack of interest is unfortunate. As a generalization, "Beginnings'" compositions, instrumentality, and lyrics are effective; the poem "Doors of Sleep" by Alice Meynell sets the stage for the entire album. On "Doors of Sleep" and "Lost Symphony," the vocals are fine. With White at the drums, Howe performs all other instruments on the album opener. Perhaps the direct means of appreciating Howe's first album lies in the instrumentals "Beginnings" and "Nature of the Sea." With orchestration by Patrick Moraz, "Beginnings" certainly draws upon the "symphonic" in "prog." I would also add "chamber" and "neo-Baroque." One might consider "Beginnings" to be Howe's "answer" to the chamber orchestra on "Time and a Word." Through this piece, Howe displays his studied approach to classical guitar and to the use of the volume pedal. Although not orchestral, "The Nature of the Sea," gives us further insight into the compositional character of Steve Howe's imagination in the mid-Seventies. With an ensemble of players found only on this album's song (Malcolm Bennett, bass, David Oberle, drums, and Graeme Taylor, guitar), Howe exemplifies the "ebb and flow" of an ocean, rendering a microcosm of "Tales from the Topographic Oceans."Considering "Will 'O' The Wisp," one can visualize Howe, Moraz, and White in the studio contemporaneously with "Relayer" or shortly thereafter. With Moraz' mellotron, Howe parallels the ephemeral character of love's relationships with the paranormal, "Will 'O' The Wisp."Perhaps "Lost Symphony" is the truly solid, single piece on "Beginnings." Here, we venture into jazz with the saxophone and productive lead vocals by Howe. As with "Will 'O' The Wisp," Moraz and White support."Beginnings" provides us with an authentic window into the creative mind of Steve Howe in the mid-Seventies. For those of us who have been given the "gift of time," we can perceive the origins of the narrative of Howe's musical journey.

items.body: Review by Atri Isla — Images and Words is my‑favorite album. On this record, Dream Theater perfectly blends progressive ideas with heartfelt emotional expression. The instrumental arrangements are intricate yet full of beauty. Pull Me Under is a progressive‑metal track with pop‑oriented qualities. I am deeply impressed by the atmosphere built within its intro.Another Day delivers magnificent emotional expression, and its solo is absolutely breathtaking.Metropolis Pt.1 "The Miracle and the Sleeper" is a brilliant narrative piece. It lays out the outline and key hints for the whole Metropolis story, which later inspired the creation of Metropolis Pt. 2.The closing track Learning to Live, in my opinion, is the most underrated song on the album. James LaBrie's vocal performance here is simply stunning.To sum up, Images and Words pioneered a brand‑new creative paradigm for progressive metal and marks the starting‑point of modern progressive metal. Its power of emotional expression stands nearly unrivaled among works of this genre.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — La Maschera Di Cera offers three expansive tracks that, much like a candle flame, burn slowly, creating the illusion that the wax remains in place rather than dripping down. Il Tempo Millenario, the first of the suites, opens with keyboards taking the lead, backed by a powerful bass-and-drums tandem reminiscent of the Yes lineup featuring Squire, Wakeman, and Bruford. Later, as Alessandro Corvaglia sings in his native tongue, accompanied only by acoustic guitar and Martin Grice's flute, the music shifts to an intimate atmosphere that embraces Italian tradition. Yet another side of that tradition also emerges: one defined by intricate rhythms evoking unexplored, inhospitable landscapes, driven by keyboard lines that resemble choral vocals punctuated by the drums.When the saxophone enters, also played by Martin Grice, the sound takes on not only a jazzy feel but also a dark quality through the keyboards; the bass and piano then come to the fore amidst a shifting, atmospheric soundscape... much like the very shape of melting wax: capricious and unpredictable.There is a rock edge to Alessandro Corvaglia's voice that complements the music's solemnity and its grandiose keyboard arrangements, which later take on a darker tone through the electric clavichord and electric guitar, achieving operatic atmospheres akin to Banco del Mutuo Soccorso. Much like that band, a free-jazz passage follows, reworking the same melody in a different key; and although Alessandro is not a tenor like Francesco Di Giacomo, he rises to the challenge admirably.Il Cerchio del Comando opens with keyboards reminiscent of the Van Der Graaf Generator that made a triumphant comeback in the 2000s as a trio. The flute then introduces a more pastoral feel, though Alessandro's vocals infuse the track with a groove blending rock, funk, and soul, recalling the acoustic side of bands like Delirium, complete with flute and Mellotron. In fact, Martin Grice had been in Delirium in the 70s."Vacuo Senso" has an overwhelming opening; following the Mellotron, bass, and flute, it erupts with saxophone and electric guitar until keyboard interludes suspend the melody, creating a strange sense of oxygen deprivation, as if one were set adrift in deep space. Echoes of King Crimson, Van der Graaf, and opera are present, yet when the guitar and piano enter, delicate counterpoints, reminiscent of Premiata Forneria Marconi, wrap the dark universe in silk and bathe it in light. The piano and bass move forward warmly, crafting an endearing melody that proves the band's ability to evoke diverse modos, much like the hues wax takes on once it dries. As if that weren't enough, an improvised jazz passage follows featuring bass, piano, and drums; it retains a melodic core, and the addition of the saxophone completes the picture, including a nod to John Coltrane's "My Favorite Things."The surprises keep coming, as a keyboard solo takes center stage, reminiscent of a Canterbury-scene album or a blend of Soft Machine and Supersister, before the saxophone steers the jazz-rock sound into full-on rock territory (a feat they mastered even without guitars). Then, an atonal keyboard passage shifts into piano, heralding the conclusion of a magnificent work; it evokes the feel of a Genesis suite, carrying a melancholic, reflective air, like a retrospective look at events past, leaving no space unfilled, much like light bouncing off windowpanes after the candle has been extinguished.

items.body: Birmingham MC Admiral Jerry, born Jerry Butler, cut “Up and Coming MC” and “Demonstrate” with UB40 in 1985. He is back with “Chant Down Babylon”, out on Windrush Day, 22 June, the date the HMT Empire Windrush docked at Tilbury in 1948. Butler grew up in Handsworth, a first-generation Black Briton of Jamaican heritage. Grammar school and a private education came next. The racism did not. “Growing up in Handsworth as a first-generation Black Briton, I experienced plenty of racist attitudes at grammar school and throughout my education,” he says. “This song is for oppressed people everywhere who are hoping and striving for a better tomorrow.“ The lyrics name Kunta Kinte, George Floyd and the Windrush Generation. Jerry works the riddim as a toaster, chatting across a roots reggae backing in the old sound system manner. Aldo Dice produced the track at his Farda Dice Studios in Birmingham for The Empire Windrush EP, with Sovereign Tugz and See No Equal on the mix and master. Jah Mission, the Amsterdam production house, shot the video across Birmingham and London. It settles on the Benjamin Zephaniah mural in Handsworth Park, unveiled in honour of the poet and activist on Windrush Day in 2024, the year after his death. More music from Jerry arrives in early 2027. Stream “Chant Down Babylon” HERE The post Daily Discovery: Admiral Jerry – Chant Down Babylon appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: And all this time I’ve been hurting for you Whatever I tried, it didn’t matter And all of my heart has been aching for you Gave all of my love – did it even matter? There is something fitting about Jonny Pierce opening his new label Abysmal Records with a song about emotional nullification. The Drums have spent fifteen years turning romantic injury into bright, economical pop, yet It Didn’t Matter, a collaboration with Mareux, carries a colder sense of aftermath. Its title lands with the bluntness of a verdict delivered after the argument has ended, when language has been exhausted, and the abandoned person is left to rearrange the evidence. Mareux’s presence is immediately legible. Aryan Ashtiani supplies synthesizers that glide with severe elegance, placing Pierce’s voice inside a glassy architecture of drum-machine momentum and bruised pop chords straight off the 80s pop charts. The production remains clean without becoming sterile; each element has room to move, while the song’s forward motion suggests somebody walking quickly through a city to avoid calling the person they are trying to forget. Pierce sings with the fragile directness that has long defined The Drums, though age has added a finer grain to his delivery. Foolishness, need, and disbelief are presented without disguise. The song describes someone trapped in the aftermath of an unequal relationship, still longing for a partner who pushed them away without releasing them. Hurt, ashamed, and angry at themselves for needing love, they question whether their devotion, sacrifice, and enduring pain ever meant anything to the person they loved. Pierce describes the session in unusually personal terms: “Not since writing my earliest music has a song come together so effortlessly. Whenever that happens, it makes me feel certain the song was meant to exist -that it needed to be here, for all of us. Mareux’s synthesizer wizardry threw me back to my teenage years, when almost everything I listened to was synthesizer-based music, especially synth-pop. His sounds, textures, and perfect pop chord changes reminded me of the soundtrack to such a tender time in my life – when I was desperate for love but just couldn’t find it, and synthesizers became the soundtrack to my sadness. This one is for those of us who keep banging our heads against the wall of another heart, only to be given nothing in return.” The collaboration grants Mareux increasing space to move beyond the viral mythology of his Cure cover, “The Perfect Girl,” showcasing him as a composer whose precise synthesizer skills elevate another artist’s songwriting and emotion. A disciplined bassline, succinct percussion, and sighing keys anchor Pierce’s confession here, letting the melody carry the emotional weight that the production keeps in elegant balance. Watch the visualizer for It Didn’t Matter below: It Didn’t Matter‘s autobiographical charge belongs to a lineage of synth-pop where polished surfaces intensify private collapse, but Pierce and Ashtiani avoid empty period detail. Their shared instincts meet in the space between romantic candour and formal restraint, producing a track that feels immediate without sounding disposable. As the first entry in a six-month series of collaborations, it gives Abysmal Records a persuasive opening statement. More importantly, it suggests that Pierce’s next phase may be built through exchange rather than isolation. It Didn’t Matter turns rejection into motion, carrying its unanswered question forward with poise, clarity and a quietly devastating hook. Catch Mareux live this autumn: 09/19 — Santa Ana, CA — Observatory Festival Grounds with AFI, Kumo 99, and L.A. Witch 10/30 — London, UK — Hootananny Brixton 10/31 — Paris/Montreuil, France — Bal Chavaux 11/03 — Athens, Greece — Floyd Live Music Venue 11/05 — Istanbul, Turkey — IF Performance Hall Beşiktaş 11/07 — Tbilisi, Georgia — Academy Follow The Drums: Instagram Spotify Follow Mareux: Website Instagram YouTube Facebook TikTok Bandcamp The post “All This Time I’ve Been Hurting for You” — Mareux and The Drums Collaborate on New Single “It Didn’t Matter” appeared first on Post-Punk.com.

items.body: Hey pals, we’re back! Thanks for sticking with us through some post-Terminus hiatus action, we needed a couple of days to rest and recoup before jumping back into the regular posting schedule, this short week notwithstanding. And hey, the upside of all of this is that we’re unusually amped to dig in on some new releases, the after-effects of seeing a ton of great music (as outlined on last week’s podcast in excruciating detail). That’s a good lead-in to this stacked edition of Tracks! Bestial Mouths doing the Bestial Mouths thing Boy Harsher, “Hard Beat” We’ve been following Boy Harsher since around the release of the first EP, and seeing them become such an enormous phenomenon with legions of fans and scads of imitators has been something of a trip. With that said, it was obvious that the duo couldn’t (and more importantly, wouldn’t) just rehash their most popular sounds and songs on their next LP, which is where “Hard Beat” comes in. Yeah, you can def hear classic BH in it, but you’re also getting a healthy dose of their interest in electropop and some more smooth and even housey vibes that differentiate it. We’ll certainly be discussing Get Mean when it drops in September, stay tuned. GET MEAN by Boy Harsher Bestial Mouths, “Conjure” Bestial Mouths have not-so-quietly become of the true stalwarts of modern darkwave, avoiding many of the broader trends and following their own gnarly, uncomfortable and often very fraught muse. The forthcoming album Dead Lines is produced entirely by band member Brant Showers, and you can definitely hear aspects of his sound design from AAIMON and SØLVE in “Conjure”, but it’s entirely in service of project mastermind Lynette Cerezo’s powerful, terrifying voice and presence. Stunning cut, and no doubt a precursor for more ill winds yet to come. DEAD LINES by Bestial Mouths Purest Form, “Animal” LA trio Purest Form look to be shooting for the moon with their forthcoming EP on Dais. Lead single “Animal” is a bracing mix of super-processed metal chug and 90s electronica at large, a formula that’ll be catnip to rivets of a certain generation still pining after quality KMFDM releases, but will likely offer fresh contrasts and new avenues for younger kids still finding their bearings in emergent apocalypses. RESISTANCE by PUREST FORM Ratio Strain, “Exorcism (Iszoloscope remix)” Hot on the heels of her excellent performance at Terminus, we have a new single from San Diego’s Ratio Strain. The lineup of remixers taking on the track “Exorcism” reflects a lot of Ratio Strain’s specific take on modern instrumental industrial and rhythmic noise, emphasizing dancefloor appeal and big textures in equal measure. Hence why you get some acid chaos from Hex Wolves, bass leaning sound design from Zer0signal, and a hot dose of inhuman ambience from Iszoloscope, the grandmaster of that particular sound. Exorcism: Possessed by Ratio Strain The Axiom Divide, “The Halls Of Amenti” The Axiom Divide is a brand-spanking new project, but look beneath the surface (as in the throwback cyber-mapping of Egyptian mysteries on the album art) and things might be a bit more familiar. Threads of frontman Jay Tye’s work in long-tenued COP act Soil & Eclipse can definitely be teased out in this melodic and ethereal blend of futurepop, synthpop, and Euro styled electro at large. The Halls of Amenti : Remixes by The Axiom Divide Anaxia, “Laser Star” A new side project from Rich Oddie of Canadian legends Orphx and Alex Pi, the taster cuts from Anaxia’s first EP speak to a controlled mastery of mood and mode. Finding commonalities between EBM, synthpunk, and post-punk and boiling their rhythmic elements down to the core, the pair flesh that skeleton out with anxious pads and squalls, taking the core elements of minimal wave to paradoxically smothering excess. Maska by Anaxia The post Tracks: August 4th, 2026 appeared first on I Die: You Die.

items.body: German electronic pop project Arsine Tibé and vocalist Suzanne Letting release the four-track concept mini-album “Reclaimed” on August 7, 2026. The digital release is a collaboration between Arsine Tibé, the solo project of Manfred Thomaser, and Letting, and centers on the experience of a woman who has survived violence, told in the first person. Thomaser describes the record’s subject as a widespread problem: “Violence against women and girls is one of the most widespread and common human rights violations worldwide.” He adds that the first-person narrative structure was chosen deliberately, to create “an immediate – and therefore very emotional – connection to the subject.” The mini-album’s main track is “Ghost Doorway”. Its official video goes online on August 7 at midnight CET, on the same day as the digital release. Arsine Tibé and Letting are also preparing a CD and vinyl edition of “Reclaimed” that will additionally include instrumental versions of all four songs; no release date for the physical formats has been confirmed yet. ‘Reclaimed’ ties into a Refuge fundraiser Arsine Tibé and Letting will donate proceeds from the CD and vinyl sales of “Reclaimed” to Refuge, the UK’s largest specialist domestic abuse organisation. Letting has separately set up a fundraising page for Refuge on JustGiving to support the same cause. About Arsine Tibé Arsine Tibé is the Lounge Noire and electronic pop solo project of Manfred Thomaser, based in Munich, Germany. Thomaser describes the project’s sound as drawing on lounge, soundtrack, ambient, new wave, electro and pop elements. He is best known as one half of !Distain, the German synthpop duo he shares with Alexander Braun, and has also worked on the projects Demokratie and The Independent Seasons. Side-Line first covered Arsine Tibé in February 2016, when Thomaser launched a mini-album under the project name, led by the track “Obligation”. Arsine Tibé has since released several collaborations with Suzanne Letting, including “Beyond the Point (feat. Suzanne Letting)” and the two-part The Lounge Noire Sessions, the second episode of which appeared on June 19, 2026. “Reclaimed” continues that collaboration and marks the pair’s first release built around a dedicated social theme, with its charity tie-in to Refuge.

items.body: Machine Command, an EBM project, released the single “Rage” on August 4, 2026. The single follows the 2026 album “Cathected” and is available on Bandcamp and Spotify. Rage by Machine Command “Rage” holds two versions of the track. The main version runs at 145 BPM as an EBM stomper, with a vocal delivery the band describes as somewhere between Rein and Anne Clarke. The second version, titled “Rage (Vocoder Dub Mix)”, uses vocodered vocals over an electrofunk arrangement the band compares to Cabaret Voltaire. Lyrically, the song addresses how social media places people into echo chambers and sets them against each other. “Rage” is the first single from a new Machine Command album, scheduled for release sometime in 2027. Machine Command describes its sound as appealing to fans of Nitzer Ebb and Portion Control, as well as newer acts such as Ultra Sunn and Ruined Conflict. On August 28, 2026, Machine Command supports Rotersand at The Helling in Utrecht, Netherlands. Additional shows are in preparation. About Machine Command Machine Command is an EBM project of Pieter Winkelaar and Annemarie Janssen. The project’s Bandcamp discography includes the albums “4PM”, “Deformed”, “Strength”, “To The Point”, “New Socialism”, “Stampfbereit”, “Two Point Zero”, “Decline and Rise Again”, “Nuke It from Orbit” and “Cathected”, the latter released March 11, 2026, alongside the EPs “Tetrarchy E.P.” and “Without Fear EP” and additional singles and remix releases. Side-Line previously covered the band’s “Affected” album. “Rage” continues that release chronology and adds the Rotersand support date to the project’s upcoming live schedule.

items.body: Princess Ugly, a post-punk and darkwave act, released the single “The Work” on August 4, 2026, together with a remix by Leæther Strip’s Claus Larsen. Both versions are available on Bandcamp, YouTube and other streaming platforms. The Work by Princess Ugly Lyrically, “The Work” presents what the band describes as an existential, ontological horror built on EBM-influenced instrumentation, addressing a compulsion to work and create that ultimately turns the created thing into something that stalks and controls its maker. The official video for “The Work” is embedded below. The single is accompanied by a remix from Leæther Strip‘s Claus Larsen. Princess Ugly describes the “Leæther Strip Remix” as a dense, infectious reinterpretation with a biting electro-industrial groove. The remix is also on Bandcamp and has its own video. About Princess Ugly Princess Ugly are J. Christopher-Rome (words, vocals) and Christopher Moncrieffe (music, instruments), based in Portland, Oregon. The project began as a solo effort from J. Christopher-Rome with a first album released in 2006; Christopher Moncrieffe joined in 2007, and the pair released two albums as a duo, “The Past, One Second At A Time” (2010) and “It Should Be Clear By Now” (2012). After a hiatus, Princess Ugly returned in 2021 with a run of singles and EPs that leaned further into post-punk and goth influences, starting with “Hunger” (2021) and continuing through “Start Below” (2022), “An Individual Soul” (2023), “Break Every Room” (2023), the EP “Death After Life” (2023), the EP “Bring the Axes” (2024) and the single “The Out” (2025). The band also appeared on the Belgian label Spleen+’s post-punk box set “Resurgence” (2025). “The Work” and its Leæther Strip remix follow that run of singles and mark the band’s latest release.

items.body: In a relatively short period of time—the band was only formed in 2020—the Italian act They Die has established itself as a notable presence within the broad spectrum of Dark-Wave and Post-Punk. With their fourth album, they return with a conceptual work exploring themes such as illusion, self-deception, manipulation, and personal transformation. At its core, it is also about removing the masks we wear and confronting reality. It is a deeply poignant subject matter that the duo has translated into nine dark and compelling tracks. The guitars create a bleak, almost apocalyptic atmosphere, while the synth lines introduce melancholic melodies that become particularly infectious during the choruses. The songs shift between slower, more atmospheric passages and faster, more dynamic moments, yet the overall mood leaves the listener with a persistent sense of tension and unease. The deep, carefully produced vocals further enhance the feeling of ‘Weltschmerz’ that permeates the album. Thematically, ‘Smoke And Mirrors’ is certainly not an album that leaves the listener with a sense of carefree optimism. However, beneath the darkness, the songs reveal a glimmer of hope. Perhaps there really is a light shining in the distance after all?! Once again, They Die prove that darkness can be a powerful source of inspiration for creating deeply moving and outstanding compositions. (Rating:8). Listen to “No Face”: No Face by They Die About They Die They Die is an Italian electro duo founded in 2020 by Giorgio Ricci, previously known for Templebeat (Dynamica-Machinery, Sub/Mission, 21st Circuitry). Unlike the 90s Electro/EBM sound of Templebeat, They Die pursues a darker, more Gothic-leaning Dark-Wave and Post-Punk direction. The project released its debut album “Emptiness Prevails” in July 2022, followed by “Black Magic” in February 2024 on Swiss Dark Nights. “Smoke And Mirrors”, the band’s fourth album, continues that release chronology on the same label.

items.body: Last Friday, Nottingham's Beyond Grace released the third and final installment in their Welcome to the New Dark Ages series, an EP trilogy set to hit the shelves physically as a full-length album later this year. Andrew Walmsley, Ed Gorrod, Tim Yearsley, and Chris Morely have been working on this technical death metal saga since November 2023, releasing each segment independently and intermittently amongst a stable output of singles. Just under a year after part one, its sequel came out, and this July, the line concludes. Welcome to the Dark Ages. Part III tracks the formula of the previous releases: three songs per extended play, with a total runtime of thirteen to fourteen minutes, hosting universally reliable death metal.Part III, acting as the ceremonial effort, should be the episode listened to first to get the freshest taste of the band. Guest vocalist Bethany "Beef" Pitts of social justice thrash collective Transgressive lends the opening track, "Radium Angels," a mean, modern attitude and pairs nicely with softer cleans and metallic instrumentation. Following that, deathcore vibes radiate from "Reign of Error," mainly coming from the slow, yet not-over-the-top breakdown. "First As Tragedy" completes the recording with another short and sweet offering.Part II and Part I follow suit in solidity, with Part II tapping deeper into proggy rhythms and moodier atmospheres, and I displaying an edgier version of Beyond Grace, prone to experimentation and evolution. If you crave three small, back-to-back injections of nice English metal totalling no longer than a regular LP, Hey! Listen to Beyond Grace!

items.body: A "groovy, mid-tempo style known for its exaggerated bouncy rhythm and common pornographic themes” is RateYourMusic’s general description for pornogrind. An offshoot of goregrind, pornogrind is not much more than what you just read. As a microgenre, it takes the already off-putting genre of goregrind (death metal-meets-grindcore-meets-preversion), and further integrates intense sexual and violent themes, a majority of the time both. I grew up with virtually zero internet supervision: on the off-chance one device was taken away, I’d resort to YouTube'ing music on any other means possible: even my Nintendo 3DS. I remember when even that was confiscated after rather suggestive rap music videos littered my search history. My time as a late teenager in the metal field—predominantly as a reviewer—has certainly built my character and provided me with some outstanding campfire tales, as I’ve seen things most anyone would never want or need to, ever. This ranges from adult content of various extremities to, to a significantly lesser extent, gore. Faintly, I recall stumbling across famous clips of violent movies, coincidentally right before bedtime. This bleeds into my experiences with pornogrind, or whenever I’m shipped a promo of a grind record, as it always results in temporary prayer to whoever’s in charge that the gore–no matter how explicit it may be–is illustrated. That gore I can tolerate, because at least it’s not genuine. Most metalheads have unfortunately stumbled across Mayhem’s infamous live album cover depicting the vivid aftermath of lead vocalist Dead’s suicide. Hell, I’ve seen it plastered on black Gildan t-shirts on TikTok. Images like these will always irk me harder than any, say, Cannibal Corpse cover, because at least theirs is illustrated. Yes, I’m not thrilled about seeing dead fetuses strung up by meat hooks or corpses mid-fellatio, but I reiterate, at least it’s illustrated. My appreciation may even flourish if it's allegorical, artistically evocative, or inventive in a way of an original presentation of the macabre. This is exactly why progressive metal is my rendezvous genre, as colorful, modern demonstrations (see Voyager - Colour in the Sun or ERRA - Silence Outlives the Earth) are, besides philosophical or literary subjects, the norm. I can waste hours leafing through progressive metal album covers without fear of scarring myself, and this practice is directly rooted in my time with progressive rock, a genre that took my younger teen years in a chokehold. Fantastical, sprawling landscapes, all hand-drawn by talented virtuosos . Alas, relating to the topical genres, goregrind is brimming with bare-bones, graphic photography, often medical (band names most likely named after whatever operation is depicted), and other gory shit, but pornogrind is where the boundaries once thought to be immovable hit the unstoppable object. In preparation for this issue, I want to elucidate that I do not solely devote my time to sifting through these albums and their covers, nor if I were to, would I relish it. My prefrontal cortex has already molded through phases unknown, and I'm sure in no time it will again.Pornogrind’s birth began with Gut, a Germanic group that blended death metal with grindcore-length bouts of brutality and incredibly reprobate ideas. Their 1991 demo tape, Drowning in Female Excrements, is credited as the first pornogrind release, and their first longplay, Odour of Torture, picturing a woman using her breast as a pin cushion (yeowch!), is the premier pornogrind album, signed to a one-man label named Regurgitated Semen Records (a one-man label still active, currently supporting five bands). No, I haven’t listened to it, and I most likely never will. Thirty-nine tracks, forty-four minutes: time I’ll dedicate to other metal projects not concerning “Triple Penetration” or “The Taboo Room.” Their ski mask-clad appearance acted as a foundation for the physical aesthetics of the acts taking part in pornogrind, and it’s not surprising that patrons often shield their faces–their digital footprint can always be traced. Since Gut’s heyday, RateYourMusic has catalogued 803 pornogrind releases, Gut being the mainstay for the next two chronologically. The highest-rated album on RateYourMusic for the genre is our good friend Gut’s 2020 LP Disciples of Smut, receiving a 3.42/5 from 262 ratings. Another well-renowned website, AOTY (Album of the Year), ranks the same: Disciples of Smut, with a 75/100 from twenty-five ratings. I can see why this record is comparably prevalent: the artwork, considering the genre, is rather tame; a black-and-white, crust-punk-ish display with a decrease but not abstinence, in pornographic visuals. The record’s material is also supposedly watered down by standard death and black metal influences, rendering it accessible to the broader metal community. Sadly, my morbid curiosity and thirst for knowledge took the best of me, and I ultimately caved and glanced at the top ten records of the genre. Thankfully, it’s fairly safe to do, and there are a couple of positive visual surprises. The second “greatest” pornogrind record is from Czechia’s Carnal Diafragma, unorthodoxly titled Space Symphony Around Us. The cover? Asteroids crossing a reddish planetary body. One of the songs is “The Art of Nature.” Carnal Diafragma clearly defies the conventional visual standards of their style, but after a quick audio sample, their music sounds exactly like any other pornoband. Another interesting item is Plasma, which takes the bronze medal. They present a vintage comic-book style interpretation of The Tarantula’s movie poster for their 2007 release Creeping! Crushing! Crawling!. The juxtaposition of graphic novel styling with music that is both graphic and novel is an interesting observation, but nonetheless unsurprising. Moving onwards, the seventh spot goes to Rompeprop from the Netherlands with another colorful comic book impression with Gargle Cummics. The most eminent band on the list is Gutalax, which gained immense social media traction for the singer's screechy vocals and (I cannot believe I’m saying this) comparably safe-for-work, scat-themed music videos. Europe dominates in this field per metal standards: The Nordics propagate the darkest and bleakest of black metal, central Europe brings the best out of power metal, and the entirety of the North birthed the lucious melodies of symphonic metal. It seems it also produces, like any other continent, a fair share of utter garbage.So that was lovely, but the real reason why you haven’t heard of this microgenre up until now is that it’s actively fading away. The only time it really reached actual reporting was after the 2019 Dayton shooting, in which the culprit was the lead singer of a short-lived collective called Menstrual Munchies. The headline is only somewhat sensationalist, giving the audience, who probably don't listen to metal at all, a vivid taste of what pornogrind is truly about. One of the bandmates took the initiative and took all the recordings of the band, claiming that "whereas I saw it as a joke...he didn't," and further commenting that he "doesn't want to be associated with [the band]." The article also supplies an efficient abstract on the genre, covering much of the material I came across. This incident actually provoked Rolling Stone, the world's most pedestrian music magazine, to remark on the style, referencing Gut, Slipknot (yes, members of Slipknot momentarily played in a little collective titled Anal Blast/Anal of Blast), before turning the topic to gun control.Still, the fade is only a positive. By succinct, self-censored scanning, it takes no decrypter to conclude that pornogrind is misogynistic as hell. A majority of the imagery and lyrical topics are insanely degrading towards women. While the devil's advocates will browbeat me about how “shock value is shock value,” I peck right back and ask them where their morals stand. The sheer amount of unexplainable online animosity directed towards women in general should be distasteful for any metalhead. Gratefully, online music databases show quite a minute amount of 2026 pornogrind releases, a considerable cut displaying anime girls in downright despicable situations or genuinely incomprehensible visual nonsense. A majority of these recordings appear to be low quality and not worth anyone’s time. It seems that each year, the pace of production of p-grind is deteriorating, and this is partially due to influential critics reciprocating my qualms by labeling the genre as “juvenile” and “straight from the toilet.” Even Metallum, the internet's largest metal music repository, doesn't officially recognize p-grind as a genre, instead filing any affiliated group under goregrind with pornographic lyricism. Metallum, admittedly, is infamous for its questionable rules of acceptance and ability to determine if a band is actually metal (for example, Rush is accepted, yet Between the Buried and Me isn't, on account of not being "metal enough"). Still, any website ready to ignore p-grind is a smidge more credible in my view. So, I've concluded the point of why p-grind isn't an appealing genre, but why has there been such a stark decline in activity? The most reasonable explanation is the convolutedness of the microgenre's concept. I love labeling music as much as the next nerd, but as I established earlier, p-grind retains little sonic originality compared to its stylistic parent. To my trained ear, the two genres sound exceptionally identical to the point where if you played two songs (this trial would only take a minute or two, thanks to the brevity of the material), I would have a rough time discerning the two. Why would band A want to distance itself from band B if both A and B are so similar? If A is goregrind with porn-themed writing, which is already a common choice in the genre, yet doesn't explicitly label itself as the likes of B, which labels itself as strict p-grind, then who, when it comes to pure material, cares? It's a matter of labeling, and if we keep to this trend of creating new styles, the soon-to-be micromicrogenres will only pertain to one or two groups. Shit, frognoise is a thing, and it's nothing more than heavy grind with amphibian content. If I go listen to, say, TrollfesT's "Dance like a Pink Flamingo," am I listening to folk metal, or flamingo metal? It's almost natural selection nowadays, when p-grind molds back into goregrind. The band with the third-highest-rated p-grind record, Jig-Ai, slowly morphed back into regular grind after their 2006 self-titled effort. Many bands follow this pipeline, so does this signal that every p-grind band will eventually technically cease?Another culprit towards the category's decline is the blatant laziness radiating from the partakers. Take Girlcock, a Quebecois p-grind project that operates under AI-generated album covers, or Pepeka Massacre, a Brazilian entity that thrives on laughably awful NSFW cartoons, exemplifying the low effort that these artists put forth. I'm yet to hear something convincing come from the genre, because the riff-forward nature and terseness of pace limit the amount of genuine distinctness a p-grind record can produce. Surely I'm not claiming some of the instrumentalists that thrive under p-grind aren't talented, but a lot of them are clearly using this genre to effortlessly MIDI their way into the metal sphere. GarageBand is an app pre-installed on most iPhones, toyed with momentarily by most new phone users, then discarded moments later to free space. Making p-grind is shockingly easy to do on this app, and little knowledge in production is needed for one to churn out record after record on an app like this and flood online databases, inflating the album count. This doesn't actually happen, of course, as, by assumption and pattern recognition, people lazy enough to make their music this way aren't exuding much effort to log in their presence on music databases.Let us all rejoice this year that pornogrind is slowly fading into obscurity. I’ve seen enough literal and metaphorical alien things shoved into other things for the rest of my life, thank you.

items.excerpt: 2026.08.04 運命の楽器と出会う絶好の機会！ 音楽の友 編集部 月刊誌 1941年12月創刊。音楽之友社の看板雑誌「音楽の友」を毎月刊行しています。“音楽の深層を知り、音楽家の本音を聞く”がモットー。今月号のコンテンツはこちらバックナンバ... 詳しく見る 弦楽器専門店のクロサワバイオリンが、ヴァイオリンとチェロの大展示販売会「弦楽器メッセ」を8月14～16日に御茶ノ水ソラシティ カンファレンスセンター2Fで開催する。 展示会では、ヨーロッパで買い付けたフランチェスコ・ビソロッティやシメオネ・モラッシなど名高いイタリア製作家の貴重な楽器をはじめ、ドイツの深みやフランスの気品を感じる逸品など、選び抜かれた銘器が一堂に集結。知識豊かな弦楽器の専門スタッフが選定をサポートし、巡り合った理想の楽器を職人が好みに合わせた細やかなセットアップや、最終調整を行い、その場で持ち帰ることができる。そのほか、手持ちの楽器の下取りにも対応している。 また、サテライト会場のクロサワバイオリン池袋店ではヴィオラ、新大久保のコントラバス本店ではコントラバスが展示され、都内3店で個性が光る楽器が多数そろう。

items.body: 2026.08.04 室内楽の魅力を一日で味わう特別な音楽祭から、夜公演をレポート 「室内楽の環 音楽祭」が7月20日、銀座・王子ホールで初開催されました。夜公演は初来日のヴァイオリニスト、エリック・シルバーガーとブラント・フレドリクセン（ピアノ）によるデュオ・リサイタル。世界初演を含む公演の模様をレポートします。 取材・文 取材・文 伊熊よし子 音楽ジャーナリスト・音楽評論家 東京音楽大学卒業。レコード会社勤務、ピアノ専門誌「ショパン」編集長を経てフリーに。クラシック音楽をより幅広い人々に聴いてほしいとの考えから、音楽専門誌に限らず、新聞、... 詳しく見る 「昼に出会い、夜に感動が極まる一日」と題した「室内楽の環 音楽祭2026」が7月20日に銀座・王子ホールで開催された。昼公演は弦楽四重奏、公開レッスン、トランペットソロ、ピアノ五重奏から六重奏まで多彩なプログラムが組まれ、初めて室内楽を聴く人に向けてモーツァルトからジョン・ウィリアムズの作品まで紹介され、公開レッスンではどのように室内楽が作られていくのか、そのプロセスが体験できるという手法である。 夜のデュオ・リサイタルは、ヴァイオリンのエリック・シルバーガーとピアノのブラント・フレドリクセンの登場。シルバーガーは第14回チャイコフスキー国際コンクールおよび2011年マイケル・ヒル国際ヴァイオリン・コンクール入賞者としてアメリカ国内外で幅広く活躍。使用楽器は1757年製ジョヴァンニ・バッティスタ・グァダニーニ。フレドリクセンはジュリアード音楽院ムンツ賞を受賞し、舞台作品の音楽監督を務めたり教育者としても活躍している。プログラムはモーツァルト、フォーレ、R.シュトラウスのヴァイオリン・ソナタと、ウィリアム・ワイゲルの《ヴァイオリンとピアノのための3つの対話》世界初演が組まれ、作曲家のワイゲルも客席で演奏を聴き、終演後はステージで挨拶を行なった。 シルバーガーのヴァイオリンは音量豊かで、その名器を朗々と響かせ、ピアノとのコミュニケーションを図る。一方、フレドリクセンの自由闊達なピアニズムもまた弦と合わせる極意を披露するものだった。とりわけ印象的だったのはワイゲルの世界初演の作品で、解説書に綴られた作曲家の文によると、「ヴァイオリンとピアノが対等な立場で語り合うことを大切にした」とのこと。冒頭の長く引き伸ばされた「ソ」の音が幾重にも変容して何度も登場する様子が印象的だった。そのワイゲルが編曲した「さくら」がアンコールで奏され、日本の美が新たな面を見せ、のびやかな変奏がコンサートの終わりを色彩感豊かに飾った。 公演情報 「室内楽の環 音楽祭」【夜公演】 エリック・シルバーガー & ブラント・フレドリクセン デュオ・リサイタル 日時：2026年7月20日 会場：王子ホール 曲目 モーツァルト：ヴァイオリン・ソナタ 変ロ長調 K.454 フォーレ：ヴァイオリン・ソナタ 第1番 イ長調 作品13 ワイゲル：ヴァイオリンとピアノのための3つの対話 世界初演 リヒャルト・シュトラウス：ヴァイオリン・ソナタ 変ホ長調 作品18

items.body: 2026.08.04 8／27サントリーホールで砂田愛梨、小林愛実、成田達輝、石上真由子が出演！「リラックスして聴いてほしい」 毎年、東京の夏をエキサイティングに彩る現代音楽の祭典「サントリーホール サマーフェスティバル」。今年はサントリーホール開館40周年を記念して、現代音楽をもっと身近に楽しめる特別企画「時を編む響」が開催。日本初演の4作品を含む全3部からなる大規模なコンサートで、砂田愛梨、小林愛実、成田達輝、石上真由子ら、実力派ソリストが揃って出演します。この公演で指揮を担当し、企画にも携わった沼尻竜典に、各作品を楽しむヒントやソリストとの組み合わせの妙について、詳しく伺いました。 取材・文 取材・文 八木宏之 1990年、東京生まれ。青山学院大学文学部史学科芸術史コース卒。愛知県立芸術大学大学院音楽研究科博士前期課程（修士：音楽学）およびソルボンヌ大学音楽専門職修士課程（M... 詳しく見る “斬新さ”ではなく、純粋に音楽的な魅力で選曲した 今年の『サントリーホール サマーフェスティバル2026』では、サントリーホールの開館40周年を記念して、特別公演「時を編む響」が開催される。 この公演で東京交響楽団を指揮するのは、「今を生きる人にとって古典と現代音楽のあいだに隔たりはない」と語る名匠、沼尻竜典。自身も作曲家である沼尻は、長年にわたり現代音楽の指揮に取り組んできた。 カミーユ・ペパン（1990〜、フランス）、池田亮司（1966〜、日本）、ショーン・シェパード（1979〜、アメリカ）、トーマス・アデス（1971〜、イギリス）の作品の日本初演に、三善晃の《決闘》と武満徹の《リヴァラン》を組み合わせたプログラムには、現代音楽に対する沼尻の想いが込められている。 ©Ayane Shindo 沼尻竜典（指揮） 神奈川フィル音楽監督、トウキョウ・ミタカ・フィル音楽監督。1990年ブザンソン国際指揮者コンクールで優勝。国内外で数々のポストを歴任。ドイツではリューベック歌劇場音楽総監督を務め、オペラ公演、リューベック・フィルとのコンサートの双方において多くの名演を残した。ケルン、ミュンヘン、ベルリン、バーゼル、シドニーなどの歌劇場にも客演。16年間にわたって芸術監督を務めたびわ湖ホールでは、ワーグナーの主要オペラ10作品をすべて指揮した。2014年にはオペラ『竹取物語』を作曲・初演、国内外で再演されている。2017年紫綬褒章受章。 沼尻 「この公演の狙いは現代音楽を日常に寄り添うものにすることです。現代音楽のプログラムだからといって、お客様には特殊な演奏会だと思わないでいただきたいのです。 その時代にいちばん新しいことをやった“斬新さ”で作品の価値を測るのではなく、純粋に魅力的な音楽かどうかを重視して、演奏家の視点で作品を選んだので、今の時代を生きる私たちの感性に直接響く音楽を、リラックスして楽しんでいただけると思います」。 サントリーホール開館40周年記念「時を編む響」の詳細はこちら 古典も現代音楽も分け隔てなく取り組む若手演奏家をキャスティング そうした沼尻のコンセプトは、ソリストのキャスティングにも現れている。 沼尻「この演奏会では、現代音楽の専門家ではなく、普段はショパンやチャイコフスキーを演奏したり、ヴェルディやプッチーニで舞台に立っている若手をソリストに起用しました。 普段からお客様に親しみのあるソリストに演奏していただくことで、同時代の作品に対する心理的なハードルを下げることができますし、現代音楽に馴染みのない方が興味をもってくださるきっかけにもなるでしょう。今回ソリストを務めるヴァイオリンの成田達輝さんと石上真由子さん、ソプラノの砂田愛梨さん、ピアノの小林愛実さんは、古典でも現代音楽でも素晴らしい演奏を聴かせてくれる名手です。彼らの世代にはもう、古典と現代音楽を隔てる壁はありません。 昭和の昔は、どんなレパートリーにも分け隔てなく取り組んでいる演奏家が器用貧乏と揶揄されることもありました。野村克也の『生涯一捕手』のような生き方が好まれていたのですね。しかし、大谷翔平が二刀流で活躍している今、世の中の価値観も大きく変わったように思います」。 コンサートは三部で構成される。石上真由子をはじめとする実力ある若手演奏家たちが、カミーユ・ペパンと池田亮司という異なる背景を持つ作曲家の作品に取り組む第1部は、室内楽という凝縮された形態で“響き”そのものに向き合う時間となる。聴き手は音と空間との関係や、そこで生み出されるテクスチャの微細な変化に耳を澄ませる。演奏会はそこから声とオーケストラ、そして大規模な管弦楽作品へと世界が広がっていく。 ©Masatoshi Yamashiro 石上真由子（ヴァイオリン） 日本音楽コンクールなど、国内外で受賞多数。題名のない音楽会、クラシック音楽館などメディア出演多数。東響、都響、読響、日本フィル、ブラショフ国立響など内外で多数のオーケストラと共演。長岡京室内アンサンブル、アンサンブル九条山メンバー。ポラリス国際音楽祭アドバイザー。Ensemble Amoibe主宰。Music Dialogue、CHANEL室内楽、おんかつ支援アーティスト。京都市芸術新人賞、音楽クリティック・クラブ賞、大阪文化祭賞、青山音楽賞、藤堂音楽賞、京都府文化賞、京都府あけぼの賞受賞。日本コロムビア、ALTUS、キングレコード、ワオンレコードよりCD好評発売中。 第2部では三善晃「ソプラノと管弦楽のための《決闘》」と武満徹「ピアノと管弦楽のための《リヴァラン》」が取り上げられ、砂田愛梨と小林愛実がそれぞれ独奏を担当する。 そして第3部では、ショーン・シェパード「管弦楽のための《表現抽象主義》」（日本初演）とトーマス・アデス「ヴァイオリンと管弦楽のための《アリア（エア）》」（日本初演）が演奏会を締めくくり、アデス作品のソリストには成田達輝が登場する。 第2部と第3部に出演する沼尻には、特に自身が指揮する4作品について、想いを語ってもらった。第2部で取り上げられる武満と三善は、沼尻と直接交流を持った作曲家であり、とりわけ三善は沼尻の作曲の師でもある。 8月22日〜30日開催！サントリーホール サマーフェスティバル 2026 日本の現代音楽を語るのに欠かせないふたり～武満徹と三善晃 沼尻「日本初演の4曲とともに武満徹と三善晃の作品を取り上げるのは、このふたりの音楽が日本の現代音楽を語るうえで欠くことのできないものだからです。 武満さんと三善さんが活躍した時代は、日本の現代音楽に最も勢いがあった時代でした。私は桐朋学園の作曲科で三善門下の学生でしたので、あの時代の現代音楽に対するワクワクした空気を肌で感じていました。 戦後日本を代表する作曲家だったふたりですが、武満さんと三善さんが進んだ道は方向の異なるものでした。武満さんは晩年、より親しみやすい作風になっていきましたが、三善さんは生涯にわたって厳しい作風を貫きました。 作曲を独学で習得した武満さんとアカデミックに学んだ三善さんという違いもあります。武満さんには戦後の日本にアメリカなどから新しく入ってきた音楽の影響が感じられ、三善さんの音楽には強烈な戦争体験の影響が感じられます。三善さんは戦争中、川で遊んでいたときにアメリカの戦闘機の機銃掃射にあい、一緒にいた友人は亡くなったそうです。この出来事は彼の死生観に大きな影響を与えました。『生というのは死から連続していて、海面の上にたまたま現れた氷山のようなものである』というのが彼のイメージです。死者と生者の境界はあいまいだと」。 三善 晃（1933～2013） 東京都出身。平井康三郎に作曲とヴァイオリンを師事。東京大学文学部仏文科在学中、日本音楽コンクール作曲部門第1位（1953）、『ピアノと管弦楽のための協奏交響曲』で尾高賞、文化庁芸術祭奨励賞を受賞（54）。パリ国立高等音楽院に留学しシャラン、ガロワ゠モンブランに師事（55～57）。『ピアノ・ソナタ』（58）などにとりわけデュティユーへの私淑が表れている。その後は、ときに鬼気迫るような緊張感をたたえつつも、人間の実存性への温かな眼差しの伏在する音楽を創作。『レクイエム』（72）、『詩篇』（79）、童声を効果的に用いた『響紋』（84）からなる反戦三部作、90年代後半以降の『焉歌・波摘み』（98）をはじめとする、熟練した書法による管弦楽曲で確固たる地位を確立。60年代から晩年に至るまで創作された多数の合唱曲は、国内のさまざまな合唱団に愛唱されており、ピアノ教則本『メソード』（97）および自身の名を冠したコンクールを通して、ピアノ教育界に与えた影響も大きい。オペラ『支倉常長〈遠い帆〉』により第31回サントリー音楽賞を受賞（2000）。桐朋学園大学学長（1974～95）、東京文化会館館長（96～2004）。日本芸術院会員（1999）、文化功労者（2011）。［平野貴俊］ 武満 徹（1930～96） 東京に生まれる。15歳ころに陸軍の宿舎でリュシエンヌ・ボワイエの『聞かせてよ愛の言葉を』を聴いて音楽に目ざめ、1948年から清瀬保二に作曲を師事。51年、瀧口修造、湯浅譲二らと芸術家団体「実験工房」を結成、劇音楽、放送用音楽、テープ音楽も発表する。たまたま耳にしたストラヴィンスキーが称賛した『弦楽のためのレクイエム』（57）、IMC（国際音楽評議会）国際現代作曲家会議でそれぞれ第5位、最優秀作品賞を受賞した『環礁』（62）、『テクスチュアズ』（64）、そしてニューヨーク・フィルハーモニック創立125周年を記念して委嘱された琵琶、尺八、オーケストラのための『ノヴェンバー・ステップス』（67）で国際的な評価を確立、日本の作曲家として未曾有の名声を獲得した。前衛的技法を独自に応用した60年代までの作品は、ときに峻厳に響くが、70年代後半以降のとりわけ水、夢、雨に着想を得た作品では、瑞々しく豊麗で耽美的な響きを追求。ポップで洒脱な「うた」のシリーズ、100以上の映画、放送用音楽の作曲、現代音楽祭「今日の音楽祭」の企画・構成（73～92）、サントリーホールの国際作曲委嘱シリーズの監修（86～98）を通して、日本の音楽文化に果たした貢献は多角的かつ厖大である。［平野貴俊］ 砂田愛梨が本拠地イタリアからコンテンポラリーを歌いに来ることの価値 沼尻「《決闘》にも、そうした三善さんの厳しさが感じられます。私はこの作品を20年以上前に天羽明惠さんとレコーディングしていますが、今回は砂田愛梨さんを独唱に迎えて演奏します。 砂田さんとは《カルメン》で共演したことがありますが、盗賊の女、フラスキータを演じる砂田さんの非常によく飛ぶ声は《決闘》にピッタリだと思いました。現在彼女はイタリアを拠点にオペラ歌手として活躍されていますが、そういう方がコンテンポラリーの作品を演奏することに大きな意義があると思っています。彼女はこの演奏会のためだけに5日間、日本に帰ってきます」。 @Satoru Masuko 砂田愛梨（ソプラノ） 東京音楽大学卒業、同大学院修了。第4回ジュディッタ・パスタ国際オペラ歌唱コンクール第2位、第94回日本音楽コンクール第1位など受賞歴多数。イタリア・サッサリ市立歌劇場でデビュー後、イタリアの様々なプロダクションに出演を続ける。また日本では、日生劇場『連隊の娘』マリー、新国立劇場『ジャンニ・スキッキ』ラウレッタ、高崎芸術劇場『カルメン』フラスキータで出演したほか、コンサートソリストとして国内各地のオーケストラとも共演。今後は新国立劇場『ウェルテル』ソフィー、日生劇場『ドン・ジョヴァンニ』ドンナ・アンナなどで出演予定。ミラノ在住。 武満徹《リヴァラン》に小林愛実の音楽性が重なった 沼尻「武満さんは三善さんと同じように戦争を体験している世代ですが、創作においては特に晩年、人間同士の繋がりを描く、温かで柔らかい表現を追求しました。武満さんの音楽からは戦後日本の生気が聞こえてくるようです。 《リヴァラン》を指揮するのは今回が初めてなのですが、2006年2月にサントリーホールで開催された『NHK交響楽団 武満徹メモリアルデー・コンサート』でウラディーミル・アシュケナージさんがこの作品を弾き振りした際に、副指揮者を務めた経験があります。本番ではピアノの脇に座って譜めくりもしました（笑）。このときに、作品をじっくりと勉強したので、いつか自分も指揮をしてみたいと思っていました。 今回小林愛実さんにソロをお願いしたのは、彼女の演奏するロマン派の作品、とりわけショパンを弾くときの音やスタイルが《リヴァラン》にとても合うと思ったからです。ショパン・コンクールの入賞者として、普段からショパンをたくさん弾いている小林さんの音楽性が、武満の作品でどのように作用するのか、とても楽しみです」。 ©HOSOO CO., LTD. 小林愛実（ピアノ） 2021年10月、第18回ショパン国際ピアノコンクール第4位入賞。7歳でオーケストラと共演、9歳で国際デビューを果たす。ブリュッヘン指揮18世紀オーケストラ、ソヒエフ指揮ミュンヘン・フィルハーモニー管弦楽団など多数のオーケストラと共演。10年に14歳でEMI ClassicsよりCDデビュー。24年11月にCD『シューベルト：4つの即興曲 作品142、ピアノ・ソナタ第19番 ハ短調、ロンド イ長調（連弾）他』をワーナークラシックスよりリリース。22年3月、第31回出光音楽賞受賞。 サントリーホール開館40周年記念「時を編む響」の詳細はこちら 今後日本でも注目が高まる ショーン・シェパード 第3部のショーン・シェパードとトーマス・アデスは、ともに今日の現代音楽界でとりわけ高く評価されている作曲家だ。シェパードは2027年度の「武満徹作曲賞」の審査員に内定しており、今後日本でも注目が高まることが予想される。 アデスも2020年度の「武満徹作曲賞」で審査員を務め、2021年1月に開催された同賞関連企画「トーマス・アデスの音楽」では、コロナ禍で来日が叶わなかったアデスに代わり、沼尻が指揮台に立った。その際にソリストを務めたのが成田達輝であり、録音を聴いたアデスは沼尻と成田の演奏を絶賛したと伝えられる。 そんなふたりが、今回アデスの作品で再共演を果たす。 沼尻「シェパードさんに関心を持ったのは、私が尊敬する指揮者のケント・ナガノさんが、彼の作品を高く評価していたからでした。今回のプログラムをサントリーホールのスタッフの皆さんと検討していた際、候補のなかにシェパードさんの作品を見つけて、これは良い機会だと迷わず選びました。 シェパードさんの音楽には奇を衒ったところがなく、今回演奏する《表現抽象主義》もある意味正統的なオーケストレーションが際立つ作品です。そこから生み出される品格あるサウンドは、サントリーホールの響きとも相性が良いと思います」。 ©Jennifer Taylor ショーン・シェパード（1979～ ） リノ（ネバダ州）出身。インディアナ大学でファゴットと作曲を学び、ジュリアード音楽院修士課程を経て、コーネル大学大学院博士課程でロバート・シエッラとスティーヴン・スタッキーに師事。2012年、ニューヨーク・フィルハーモニックのクラヴィス新進作曲家賞を受賞、その後アンサンブル・アンテルコンタンポランやWDR交響楽団により作品が初演されるなど、ヨーロッパでも知られるようになる。その音楽は饒舌さと生命力、都会的で洗練された感触を特徴とする。そうした美点を顕著に示すのが、各楽器群の音色を細やかに際立たせ、明快で立ち上がりのよい響きを作りだした小管弦楽のための『これらの特殊な事情』（09）と、色彩感のある和声も加えて、力動性と抒情性を両立させた管弦楽曲『表現抽象主義』（17）である。近年は内省的な雰囲気も採りいれて作風を多面化させており、23年、カーネギーホールにてケント・ナガノ指揮ハンブルク州立フィルハーモニー管弦楽団によって初演された独奏チェロと独唱、合唱を伴うオラトリオ『晴れた日に』はそうした傾向を表す一作である。同年、アメリカ芸術文学アカデミーのチャールズ・アイヴズ生活賞を受賞。2027年度武満徹作曲賞審査員。［平野貴俊］ アデス作品での共演が忘れられない成田達輝 今回の《アリア》でもピュアな音楽性に期待 沼尻「トーマス・アデスさんが国際的に注目を集めるきっかけとなった、サイモン・ラトルのベルリン・フィルハーモニー管弦楽団芸術監督就任披露公演での《アサイラ》を、私は現地で聴いていて、リハーサルも見学しました。その後も『コンポージアム』（東京オペラシティの同時代音楽を中心とするフェスティバル）で彼の代役を務めたり、なにかと縁の深い作曲家です」。 ©Marco Borggreve トーマス・アデス（1971～ ） ロンドン出身。ケンブリッジ大学で学ぶ（1989～92）。管弦楽曲『アサイラ』（97）でロイヤル・フィルハーモニー協会賞、2000年には史上最年少でグロマイヤー作曲賞を受賞するなど、短期間で国際的名声を確立。指揮者、ピアニストとしても活躍する。スキャンダラスな題材にもとづく室内オペラ『顔に白粉を』（1995）も成功し、その後創作された2つのオペラ『テンペスト』（2003）、『皆殺しの天使』（15～16）も再演が重ねられるなど、現代もっとも人気のあるオペラ作曲家のひとりでありながら、あらゆる形態の作品を発表している。ポピュラー音楽を含む多様なジャンル、時代の音楽を参照するその作品は、一作ごとに異なる様相をみせるが、室内アンサンブルのための『生きた玩具』（1993）などの初期作品にみられる皮肉っぽさや諧謔味は、後の『ピアノ協奏曲』（2018）やヴァイオリンと管弦楽のための『おとぎ話の踊り』（20）にも現れている。またシュルレアリスト的とも評される夢幻的な響きは、近年では管弦楽曲『ポラリス』（10）、『夜明け』（20）、ヴァイオリンと管弦楽のための『アリア（エア）』（21～22）において、線的で緻密なテクスチュアのなかで実現されている。［平野貴俊］ 沼尻「今回演奏するアデスさんの《アリア》は、『シベリウスへのオマージュ』という副題からもわかるように、透明度の高い作品で、誤解を恐れずに言えば、東山魁夷の絵のような音楽ではないかと思っています。やはりアデスさんが住むイギリスは、フィンランドと同じく、北海道より北にある国なんだなとも感じます。 ソリストを務めてくださる成田達輝さんは、2021年にご一緒した東京オペラシティの「トーマス・アデスの音楽」における『ヴァイオリン協奏曲《同心軌道》』の名演が忘れられません。とても難しい作品でしたが、どんなに複雑なパッセージでも、成田さんが弾くと音楽として心にすっと入ってきました。彼の演奏はどこまでも感性豊かで、こうやって現代の作品を弾ける人がいるのかと驚いたのを覚えています。共演した東京フィルのメンバーも、成田さんのソロを絶賛していました。今回も成田さんのピュアで自然な音楽性が存分に活きるだろうと期待しています」。 ©Marco Borggreve 成田達輝（ヴァイオリン） 2010年ロン゠ティボー国際コンクール第2位、12年エリザベート王妃国際音楽コンクール第2位。国内外の指揮者・オーケストラと多数共演し高い評価を得るとともに、リサイタルやジャンルにこだわらない様々なアーティストとの室内楽においても圧倒的なテクニックと多彩な表現力を披露している。現代作曲家とのコラボレーションも多く、22年9月には坂本龍一のプライベート録音に参加し『ソナタ』などを演奏。使用楽器は、A. ストラディヴァリ「Tartini」1711年製（宗次コレクションより貸与）。 『サントリーホール サマーフェスティバル 2026』では、今回掘り下げた「時を編む響」のほか、沼尻が若手演奏家たちとともに立ち上げる「アンサンブル・ゴーフォーイット」の第1回演奏会も開催され（8/22 ブルーローズ［小ホール］）、沼尻の長年の音楽活動を通して蓄積された、現代音楽に対する豊富な経験が、新しい世代の音楽家たちへと継承される。そうした試みは日本の音楽界の未来に確かなインパクトを残すだろう。 沼尻「現代音楽のコンサートには、滅多に演奏されない作品が聴ける貴重な機会であることを前面に押し出して、イベントのように盛り上げていくものも少なくありません。そうしたアプローチも悪くはないのですが、ベートーヴェンやブラームスのような古典が演奏される普段のコンサートの延長として、現代の音楽を聴いていただきたいというのが私の思いです。 現代音楽を特別なものとして古典と切り離すのではなく、バッハやモーツァルトから連綿と続く音楽史の流れに連続するものとして、同時代の作品を捉えることが大切だと思っています。かつてはそれを破壊することを主眼とした作品も多く作られて、誤解も生じていると思いますが、今回取り上げる作品はいずれも音楽史の連続性が感じられるものばかりです。両日とも安心して（笑）サントリーホールへおいでください」。 「現代音楽を日常に」という沼尻の想いを受け止めて、私たちも身構えることなく、時代の響きに耳を傾けたい。 8月22日始動！「アンサンブル・ゴーフォーイット」の公演詳細はこちら 8月22日〜30日開催！サントリーホール サマーフェスティバル 2026 サントリーホール サマーフェスティバル 2026 サントリーホール開館40周年記念「時を編む響」 日時：8月27日（木）18:30開演
